title: ITPNet: Towards Instantaneous Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving

problem.claim: Autonomous-driving trajectory prediction must handle agents with very limited observed trajectory locations.

gap.claim: Existing approaches usually require sufficiently long observations, and many prediction models collapse when adequate observations are unavailable.

contributions.claim: ITPNet is a general plug-and-play approach for instantaneous trajectory prediction when only two observed locations are available.
A backward forecasting mechanism predicts latent representations of unobserved historical trajectories from two observed locations and uses them as complementary information for future prediction.
The NRRFormer module filters noise and redundancy from predicted unobserved-trajectory features and combines them with observed features into a compact query representation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on the Argoverse and nuScenes datasets reportedly show that ITPNet outperforms baselines by a large margin.
The authors report efficacy across different trajectory prediction models.

narrative_sequence.summary: Trajectory prediction is important for autonomous-vehicle safety, but existing methods generally depend on long observation histories.
Real-world occlusions and sudden appearances can leave too few observed locations for reliable prediction.
The paper defines instantaneous trajectory prediction using only two observed locations during inference.
ITPNet reconstructs latent historical information through backward forecasting and reduces noise and redundancy before future prediction.
The approach is described as compatible with existing prediction models and is reported to outperform baselines on two datasets.

source_observation.claim: When historical observations are sparse, the method reconstructs latent historical representations from the limited observations.

interpretation.claim: Inference-time information scarcity can be addressed by estimating missing historical context rather than relying only on the directly observed sequence.

application.claim: This pattern may apply to sequential prediction tasks where agents or events appear late, intermittently, or under occlusion.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether reconstructed latent history is reliable across observation noise levels, agent types, or deployment conditions.

unknowns: No quantitative performance metrics or exact improvement margins are provided.
The abstract does not identify the baselines, prediction models, data splits, or experimental settings.
Training, computational, latency, and reproducibility details are omitted.
